blocks.title: Capablanca writes
blocks.text: "The most important thing in the opening is to develop the pieces quickly. No piece should be moved more than once before development is complete, unless it is absolutely necessary."

In chess **White always moves first** and therefore has a slight initial advantage. Both players’ task in the opening is the same: bring the pieces into play as fast as possible and take control of the centre.

blocks.title: Develop the pieces quickly
blocks.text: Capablanca advises: develop knights before bishops. Don’t move the same piece twice in the opening unless forced. Every move should develop a new piece or control the centre.

blocks.title: Control the centre
blocks.text: The four central squares (e4, d4, e5, d5) are the most important on the board. Whoever rules the centre has more room to manoeuvre. Capablanca: "No vigorous attack can succeed without control of at least two central squares."

blocks.title: Protect the king — castle!
blocks.text: Castle as early as possible. A king in the open is an easy target. Capablanca himself always castled early and recommends the same to all players, especially beginners.

items.title: Bringing the queen out too early
items.text: The queen is strong, but if you bring her out early the opponent attacks her with pawns and pieces — and every attack on the queen means a lost tempo because she must flee.

items.title: Passive defence with pawns
items.text: The "Philidor" style — answering e4 immediately with P-d6 — gives the opponent free development and space. Capablanca shows how White then easily builds a superior position.

items.title: Castling too late
items.text: Every move without castling while the lines are open is a risk. The opponent can open the position and attack your king before it gets to safety.

blocks.text: Play each of White’s moves on the board — Black replies automatically along the theoretical line.
